title: A season (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hook: "To every thing there is a season"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's opening cry: hevel, breath of breaths. Your line was nothing stays in the hand. Did you loosen your grip on something? Today, the same book turns its breath into a rhythm, and the week comes to a close. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

Same afternoon, same street. On one porch, a family is setting out chairs for a party, balloons tied to the railing. Three doors down, the curtains are drawn, and cars are parked along the curb for a house of mourning. A man walks past both houses on the way to buy milk. Nobody on that street is doing life wrong. They're just in different hours of it. Kohelet has a poem for that street. It reads like a list, and it works like a clock.
screen: `A PARTY ON ONE PORCH.` → `MOURNING THREE DOORS DOWN.` → `DIFFERENT HOURS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes chapter three, in the words of the King James text: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Then the list begins. "A time to be born, and a time to die." A time to plant, and a time to pluck up. A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And it ends: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. Notice how it's built. Pairs. Every line holds two opposites, side by side, and neither one cancels the other. The poem doesn't say mourning is bad and dancing is good. It says each has its hour. Yesterday, Kohelet called everything breath. Today he hints at something steadier underneath. A little further on in the chapter he says that God hath made every thing beautiful in his time. In its time. Not every moment is beautiful on its own. But each one has a place. Readers take the poem two ways. Some find comfort: grief won't last forever, and neither will this hard stretch. Others hear a challenge: you don't choose the season, but you can ask what this one is for. Is it a time to speak, or a time to keep silence? A time to plant, or a time to wait? The poem doesn't answer for you. It just insists the question is real. There is a time for everything.
screen: `TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.` · `PAIRS OF OPPOSITES, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `EVERY THING BEAUTIFUL IN HIS TIME.` · then: `WHAT IS THIS SEASON FOR?`

segments.voice: First, a look back at this week. Mishlei and the first step through the door. Atzei chayim. Rakh. Each child's own way. The need comes first, and the history comes second. Nothing stays in the hand. Now the practice: name the season you're in. Settle, and let a pair from the poem find you. A time to plant or to pluck up. To weep or to laugh. To keep silence or to speak. Don't choose the one you wish for; notice the one that's true. Say it quietly to yourself: this is a time to... and finish the line. If you pray, you can bring that season with you into prayer. The bell holds the time.
A season. Ecclesiastes three: to every thing there is a season, pairs of opposites, each with its own hour. Today's word.
Your line: a time for everything. Today, when you meet someone in a different season from yours, mourning or celebrating, let their hour be what it is. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 belongs to Kohelet, one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and some Jews quote its 'a time to' lines at turning points in life, from celebrations to houses of mourning.
